title: Build a Simple AI Tool — Text Summarizer CLI

sections.content:
## What You'll Build

A command-line tool that takes any text file and summarizes it using Claude. By the end of this lesson you'll have a working tool you can actually use:

```
node summarize.js notes/meeting-notes.txt
node summarize.js report.txt --bullets
```

This is a real tool — not a demo. You'll be able to run it on your own files after this lesson.

## What You'll Build, Step by Step

1. Create the project and install dependencies
2. Read a file from command-line arguments
3. Send the file contents to Claude with a summarization prompt
4. Print the summary
5. Add streaming so output appears progressively
6. Add a `--bullets` flag for bullet-point summaries

Each step produces working code. If you get stuck at any step, you can ask Claude Code to help.

## The Complete Final Tool

Here is the complete `summarize.js` — read through it before building, so you understand the destination:

sections.title: Build the Text Summarizer
Workshop A — Build the Summarizer CLI
sections.content:
Build the text summariser tool described in the lesson.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code to scaffold the full project:**
```
Build a production-ready CLI tool called summarise.py that:
1. Accepts a file path or stdin as input
2. Calls the Anthropic API to summarise the content
3. Supports flags:
   --length short/medium/long (controls summary detail)
   --format bullet/prose/structured
   --model haiku/sonnet (default: haiku for cost)
4. Handles large files by chunking if needed (over 50k tokens)
5. Shows a progress spinner during processing
6. Outputs the summary cleanly, then shows token usage and cost

Write the complete implementation.
```

**Step 2 — Review the code** thoroughly before running it.

**Step 3 — Test on real files:** a code file, a document, a long email.

sections.title: Workshop B — Add Features to Your CLI
sections.content:
Extend your summariser based on real usage experience.

**Step 1 — Use the summariser on 5 real documents** from your work.

**Step 2 — Identify the most annoying limitation** in its current form.

**Step 3 — Ask Claude Code to add the feature:**
- Batch processing: `summarise.py *.txt > summaries.md`
- Output to file: `--output summary.md`
- Compare mode: summarise two files and highlight differences
- Follow-up questions: after summarising, enter an interactive mode to ask questions about the document

**Step 4 — Test the new feature** with real input.

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Ask Claude: *"Review the implementation of [new feature]. What edge cases did I miss? What would break with unusual inputs?"*

sections.title: Workshop C — Test Your Tool End-to-End
sections.content:
Write tests for your CLI tool.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code to write a test suite:**
```
Write a pytest test suite for summarise.py that:
1. Tests each --length option produces different output lengths
2. Tests --format produces correctly formatted output
3. Tests that file-not-found is handled gracefully
4. Tests that very short input (under 10 words) is handled gracefully
5. Tests that the token count in output is a positive integer

Use pytest-vcr or mock the Anthropic API calls so tests don't cost real money.
```

**Step 2 — Run the tests:** `pytest tests/ -v`

**Step 3 — Fix any failures.** Are the failures real bugs or test issues?

**Step 4 — Check coverage:** `pytest --cov=summarise`

sections.title: Workshop D — Deploy and Share Your Tool
sections.content:
Package your CLI tool for distribution.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code** to help package the tool:
```
Help me package summarise.py for distribution:
1. Create a pyproject.toml so it can be installed with pip install
2. Create a requirements.txt
3. Write a README.md with installation instructions and usage examples
4. Add a --version flag
5. Make it available as a global command: `summarise` after installation
```

**Step 2 — Install your own tool:** `pip install -e .`

**Step 3 — Test that the global command works:** `summarise README.md`

**Step 4 — Share with one colleague** and observe how they use it. What confused them? What did they want that was missing?

sections.question: Your summariser CLI works great on 5-page documents but hangs on a 200-page PDF. What is happening and how do you fix it?
options: PDFs are not supported by the API
The document exceeds the context window — you need to chunk the document into segments, summarise each, then summarise the summaries
You need a more powerful computer
sections.explanation: Every model has a context window limit. A 200-page document might be 100,000+ tokens — more than any single API call can handle. The solution is hierarchical summarisation: (1) split the document into chunks that fit within the context window (with overlap for context continuity), (2) summarise each chunk, (3) combine chunk summaries into a meta-summary. This is called the "map-reduce" summarisation pattern and is essential for handling documents of arbitrary length.

sections.question: You build a summariser that works well for English text but produces poor results for French documents. What is the most likely reason and fix?
options: Your system prompt doesn't specify the target language — add "Respond in the same language as the document" or explicitly "Respond in French" to the system prompt
French uses more tokens and you need higher max_tokens
You need a different model for non-English text
sections.explanation: Claude supports many languages but defaults to responding in English when the language isn't specified. For multilingual applications, add explicit language instructions to the system prompt: "Summarise the document in the same language it was written in." You can also dynamically detect the language of the input and add a specific instruction. Without this, Claude may respond in English even when the source document is in another language.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 11-8.** You built a real AI tool from scratch — not a tutorial copy-paste, but a working utility you can use on your own files today. You applied: SDK, file I/O, streaming, CLI argument parsing, and error handling. Next: making this tool dramatically cheaper to run at scale.
